scenes.title: Predict while ice melts
scenes.learnerAction: Use the model, complete its task, and explain what the representation shows.

content.body: Consider pure ice and liquid water together at equilibrium near one atmosphere. Predict whether adding heat must immediately raise temperature. This is a paper model. Do not heat, taste or handle boiling water for this lesson.

items.prompt: During melting while both phases remain, what happens to temperature?

options.text: It stays about 0 C while heat is absorbed.
options.feedback: Heat can change state at a constant temperature.

options.text: It must rise continuously whenever heat enters.
options.feedback: Temperature measures average kinetic energy, not all transferred energy. Melting can absorb heat without raising temperature.

scenes.title: Test the energy model on paper
scenes.learnerAction: Compare the model at 21 kJ and 355 kJ. What changed despite equal temperatures? Explain what you kept fixed.

content.body: Keep mass at 1 kg and pressure fixed. Move through the supplied energy-temperature pairs. This model experiment uses net heat added, not time. Ice warms first, then melts, then liquid warms. Water particles keep their identity. Solid particles vibrate about fixed sites; liquid particles remain close and can move past one another; gas particles are far apart.

blocks.title: Idealized heating of 1 kg of pure water

data.note: Calculated ideal model at fixed pressure near one atmosphere. Fixed mass retained with expansion allowed to maintain pressure; approximate heat capacities. Not measurements or a heating procedure.

blocks.caption: A-B ice warms; B-C ice and liquid coexist at 0 C; C-D liquid warms; D-E liquid and vapor coexist at 100 C; E-F vapor warms. Unequal horizontal intervals show different required energies. See the packet SVG for segment labels.

items.prompt: Which particle model explains an ice cube's shape and volume?

options.text: Particles vibrate about fixed positions in an open solid structure; ice has its own shape and approximately fixed volume.
options.feedback: Fixed positions allow vibration. An ice cube on a plate keeps its shape until melting.

options.text: Ice particles are motionless and have no space between them.
options.feedback: Solid particles still vibrate. Water ice has an open structure; it is not a motionless solid block at particle scale.

items.prompt: Water is poured from a cup to a bowl without spilling. What changes?

options.text: Its shape changes; volume stays essentially the same because close particles can move past one another.
options.feedback: Changing containers rearranges the same close particles. The same amount keeps nearly the same volume.

options.text: Its particles grow and the amount of water increases to fill the bowl.
options.feedback: The water particles do not grow. A liquid takes the shape of the part of the container it occupies, not necessarily the whole container.

items.prompt: Which model describes water vapor or the gases in a classroom's air?

options.text: Far-apart particles move randomly and fill available space; gas has no own fixed shape or volume.
options.feedback: Gas expands through particle movement and separation, not growth of individual particles.

options.text: Gas particles grow larger but stay in fixed positions.
options.feedback: Gas particles move rapidly in random directions and collide. They do not grow to fill the container.

scenes.title: Explain latent heat and evaporation
scenes.learnerAction: Use the model, complete its task, and explain what the representation shows.

content.body:
Latent heat is energy absorbed or released during a change of state without a temperature change in this ideal model. It changes the arrangement and separation associated with attractions between particles, rather than increasing average kinetic energy. Melting and vaporization absorb energy; freezing and condensation release it. These reversible physical changes preserve water molecules.

Evaporation happens at a liquid surface even below boiling temperature. Some surface molecules escape into the gas. Boiling forms vapor bubbles throughout the liquid at its boiling temperature for the pressure. Invisible water vapor is gas; visible mist contains tiny liquid droplets.

accessibility.textAlternative:

It changes the arrangement and separation associated with attractions between particles, rather than increasing average kinetic energy. Melting and vaporization absorb energy; freezing and condensation release it. These reversible physical changes preserve water molecules.

Evaporation happens at a liquid surface even below boiling temperature. Some surface molecules escape into the gas. Boiling forms vapor bubbles throughout the liquid at its boiling temperature for the pressure. Invisible water vapor is gas; visible mist contains tiny liquid droplets. Why can water take a cup's shape but ice keep its shape? Options: Liquid particles move past neighbors; solid particles vibrate about fixed positions.; Liquid particles grow to fill the cup..

items.prompt: Why is the melting segment flat?

options.text: Heat changes the phase while ice and liquid coexist.
options.feedback: The increasing heat coordinate shows energy still enters the sample.

options.text: The heater has stopped transferring energy.
options.feedback: A flat temperature line does not mean zero energy transfer. The sample is absorbing latent heat while it melts.

items.prompt: A wet cloth dries at 28 C. Which explanation fits?

options.text: Evaporation from its surface can occur below boiling.
options.feedback: Surface evaporation does not require boiling throughout the liquid.

options.text: The cloth must secretly have reached 100 C.
options.feedback: Boiling and evaporation are different processes. Water can leave the surface at 28 C without vapor bubbles throughout it.

items.prompt: What happens when liquid water freezes at its freezing point?

options.text: Energy leaves the water as particles settle into the solid arrangement.
options.feedback: Freezing reverses melting and releases latent heat to the surroundings.

options.text: Freezing requires heat to enter the water because cold is a substance.
options.feedback: Cold is not a substance. The water loses energy to its colder surroundings as it freezes.

items.prompt: Why can water take a cup's shape but ice keep its shape?

options.text: Liquid particles move past neighbors; solid particles vibrate about fixed positions.
options.feedback: Arrangement and motion change, not particle size or identity.

options.text: Liquid particles grow to fill the cup.
options.feedback: The particles do not grow during melting. Their arrangement and freedom of movement change.

scenes.title: Explain cooling and reversibility
scenes.learnerAction: Propose a test that distinguishes condensation from leakage without opening the cup. State what result supports each explanation.

content.body: Synthetic observations: droplets form outside a cold sealed metal cup, and a wet cloth dries at room temperature. Use particle motion and energy transfer to explain both. Consider where the outside droplets came from and how each state change could be reversed.
